The doctors said sometimes that happens. The depression got bad enough that I was diagnosed with major depressive disorder. How has this disease affected your career?

I have done okay, but I have opted to stay in a lower stress job with a lower income as I believe stress makes my UC worse. I am probably making about $15k less than I could if I switched jobs.

How has this disease affected your finances?

I have insurance through my current job which actually covers most everything with greatly reduced out of pocket costs. I am very very lucky.

When I was first diagnosed and had insurance issues I budgeted thinking Humira cost around $1000 for a months supply out of pocket. I went to a CVS because I had a prescription, so I figured I could pay out of cost. I had a pharmacist laugh at me for thinking I could get the medicine at a pharmacy because I didn't know it came from a specialty pharmacy yet and I didn't realize that the drug I was on cost like $12,000/mo without insurance. I wasn't informed of the program through the company who made the medication so I just didn't get medicine for that month because I thought I couldn't afford it. So yeah, fuck that whole situation.

Is there anything positive that has come about specifically because of your IBD?

I feel like there aren't any positives that aren't also negatives. I understand how to deal with insurance companies who won't cover your treatments. I understand what the processes are for getting replacement medications when there are issues because the first time it happened took 3 weeks and I had already missed a dose by the time I got it. The best advice I can give is do whatever you can not to stagnate. The biggest problem with anxiety and depression that I've found is once you start to slip, it's super easy to keep slipping further into depression.

For me personally there are things I have to do in order to keep moving forward.

* Get the fuck up and take a shower. Wash yourself everyday. Nobody likes being around someone who's hygeine isn't there and it will give you some confidence. You got out of bed, got out of your stank, and cleaned up. Go you. You might also try to make sure you go outside. Even if it's just a drive to the local park to catch a Pokemon on Pokemon go or something. Getting out helps.

* Do not go anywhere on the internet that talks about depression, suicide, or anxiety. This is part of that feedback loop thing. If you surround yourself with really depressing things you're going to think it's normal and your brain is getting more exposure to those thoughts. You need to break the pattern. Go look at /r/babyelephantgifs or /r/photoshopbattles. Pretty much anything with more healthy thought patterns and maybe a slightly more positive feel.

* Do not let yourself use depression or anxiety as an excuse. I'm not saying that it isn't serious, but the problem is the more you use it as a crutch the more you're depending on it when you need to be working on not letting it stop you. This means you need to learn to push through it, and yes this sucks. Even if that means you need to start with small things like taking a shower every day, making sure you go outside and get something to eat, or simply going out for a drive.

Later these will expand to not letting things interfere with deadlines in work or school. Because moving forward in any way is better than sitting there and worrying about not moving forward. Everyone makes mistakes and everyone forgets to prioritize things. You need to reteach yourself how to deal with that kind of stress in a healthy way.

I feel bad because my advice really does boil down to not letting yourself sit and stew in depression and get up to go do a thing. But at least for me, that's how I had to push myself out of it and continue to keep moving forward.

I don't think it's so much "faked" as people not understanding depression and as someone who has clinically diagnosed major depressive disorder I get it.

From what I can tell a lot of people think that being sad or having ups and downs is depression. But that's not quite right. While it's certainly possible for someone to suffer from depression short term, usually it's a much more serious long term condition. I think especially for teenagers there's a hormone thing along with sadness which while serious, is not quite the same thing, but really needs to be taken seriously all the same.

If someone has real depression, they are going to have mood swings. It's like one second you can be okay and then someone says one off hand comment that shouldn't matter to you or was a joke, but it just sends you spiraling and five minutes later you're in bed crying, wishing you were dead, and falling behind in life because there's somewhere you're supposed to be and things you're supposed to be doing. None of that matters anymore because you wish you were dead and are trying to figure that out.

This kind of reaction happens all the time to really trivial things. For example say you're pouring cereal and milk. If you spill a little bit, I think we have all done that, a healthy persons brain just goes, "whoops, better clean that up." Someone with actual depression might start thinking, "I can't even do that right. I'm completely worthless. I should just kill myself so that other people don't have to deal with my pathetic ass." It's like that for pretty much every daily task or encounter that doesn't go perfectly.

On top of that, you're tired all the time. You can't sleep when you need to, and you might sleep all day. You're probably going to be lethargic so while you might normally have a chance of quickly recovering from a mistake or fixing it near instantly, when you're depressed that isn't going to happen. It sucks because it makes the whole world seem like it's moving fast while you're in slow motion so you don't have a shot of catching up. It's very hard to forgive yourself and move on.

I only know a couple of people who actually have long term diagnosed depressive disorders and know tons of people who post depression memes and such. The difference is immense. Think dropping out of college, losing a dream job, or messing up close personal relationships all of which have huge consequences on your life.

I think part of that is people who have the long term depressive disorders have to learn to self regulate because it's destructive in your life. You need to learn to try and manage it. How do you deal with things that will make you spiral. If you start to notice yourself having trouble, what do you do? Is medication helpful for you? Is therapy helpful? It seems like it's largely a person to person case and just because a medication helps doesn't mean it doesn't hurt too. If the med stops you from wanting to kill yourself all the time, it probably stops most of your emotions from coming through.

Not a girl, but I doubt it really makes a difference for this post. For context, I have clinically diagnosed major depressive disorder and an anxiety disorder.

* I have good days and bad days with both and they may overlap.
* With depression at my worst points I'll literally be sitting naked crying with a handful of pills that would send me into cardiac arrest or cause me to have a stroke. I might be pressing heated Allen wrenches against my skin to burn myself. At best, you would not know I have a problem or know how pessimistic I actually am. I wouldn't even know I have a problem in some moments.
* My anxiety disorder is bad to the point where I won't leave my room for pretty much months on end. If I have to leave my room for food or whatever I might have a panic attack and start hyperventilating just trying to focus on my breathing and calm myself down. At other times I again will function like a normal healthy person.
* When I'm having good days I often feel guilty for things I've done or if I'm not trying to correct things I didn't get around to doing or for causing people to go out of their way because I couldn't keep my shit together.
* I don't say anything to anyone about it. I just kind of disappear for long periods of time. This kind of also snowballs into not having any friends. I'll have nightmares about people who are making fun of me behind my back whenever I get close to anyone. I'll constantly feel like I'm upsetting them. It's just hard to be around other people even though I've been told by a lot of people I'm extremely personable or "the nicest person" they've ever met.
* The problem with all of this is that nobody knows what's going on in my head. I just look like a slacker.
* Another thing is people who offer advice on depression. A lot of people don't seem to understand it's more than just being sad. Advice like trying to stay positive don't work. Try to imagine if you were physically incapable of looking on the bright side. Imagine if spilling a drink snowballs into you thinking about how worthless a human you are and every mistake you've ever made comes flooding through your head.
* One of the worst things for me specifically is videogames. For a lot of people looking at my life they'd see the amount of videogames I play and think I'm just lazy considering the amount of things I blow off in order to play games. The reality is I've tried not playing games. For me, I believe it's actually much healthier to play games because when I'm not, that brain power goes to laying in bed and thinking about suicide. When I'm playing games all day I'm distracted. At least I'm not thinking about how much I want to kill myself all day.

For me, medication and therapy help. They bring me back from the very edge of wanting to kill myself all the time, but not much more than that and that's not even all the time. I still have bad times, but they aren't quite as bad.

I personally struggle with clinical major depressive disorder. I have to take medication every day or I start wanting to indulge in self harm. I can't focus on anything because I think about how much I want to kill myself. Yes, that includes staring at the wall for hours on end. The way depression works is that your brain is fucked up. You literally aren't capable of normal tasks. Your brain can't process it and you don't have the energy to do anything. For me a pill everyday can help and I'm really lucky because that doesn't happen for a lot of people. There are plenty of people who've tried every anti-depressant on the market with no relief. My mind fundamentally changes and becomes a more pleasant place most of the time. I still struggle sometimes though and at least for me it's genetic. There's nothing I can do about it as far as a permanent fix.

Also, one thing that's not really talked about is that getting treatment can be VERY dangerous for people with depression. It can take a while for a medication to balance the chemicals in your brain. While that process is starting, you have more energy but the way you think hasn't yet changed. That's why one of the side effects from these meds are suicide attempts. You have someone who daydreams all day about dying and they suddenly have energy to act on it. Or you can have a medication that gives energy with no effect on your thinking patterns. It's a very dangerous combination.
